Non-Governmental Services Impacts
Non-governmental services have not received the detailed study necessary to specifically assess or project the capacity of these services to expand under high levels of coal production on the Crow coal resource area. However, the Northern Great Plains Resources Program studied six coal producing counties in North Dakota, Montana and Wyoming (including Big Horn County), to determine the attitudes and confidence levels of community leaders concerning the ability of the communities to adapt to increased demand for non-governmental services.
For both profit and non-profit organizations, the large majority of leaders felt that increased demands for non-governmental services could be adequate, provided, particularly if sufficient lead-time were available. In most cases, they felt that lags in meeting increased demands would be in some proportion to the rapidity and extent of development.
The severity of these lags would be highly dependent on the availability of (1) necessary facilities and equipment, (2) needed supplies and materials and (3) developing adequate staffs. The most serious of these would probably be the latter, particularly where it would entail acquiring scarce technical, professional or managerial skills.
For some non-profit organizations, financing capital and operational outlays may be difficult, particularly where a large percentage of
the funds must be generated locally. Any such difficulties could seriously increase the lag between demand and supply for such services.
